study_characteristics.study_objective: The study aimed to better understand cerebellar anatomy and its diversity in autism by examining cerebellar gray matter morphology in a large multicenter European cohort using multiple parcellation methods, statistical approaches (including normative modeling), and dimensional analyses to address inconsistent findings from previous studies.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: CERES pipeline; SUIT pipeline; FreeSurfer (quality metric: Euler number)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Visual quality check by an expert rater (CL) blind to diagnosis for all parcellation outcomes. Participants with motion artifacts and parcellation errors were excluded. Out of 607 total subjects, 127 subjects (21%) were excluded: 280 subjects with excessive head motion and low-quality anatomical images, 279 subjects with parcellation errors were excluded from the Healthy Brain Network analysis. Euler number used as quality metric. There was no difference in the proportion of individuals with autism/control subjects in excluded/included subjects; however, FSIQ and age were lower in excluded participants.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Site of inclusion included as covariate in linear models and normative modeling. Six sites included: Cambridge (Siemens Verio), London (GE Discovery mr750), Mannheim (Siemens TimTrio), Nijmegen (Siemens Skyra), Rome (GE Signa HDxt), and Utrecht (Phillips Achieva/Ingenia CX). In normative modeling, site was included as a covariate in the Gaussian process regression model along with age, sex, FSIQ, and ICV. Meta-analytic approach was used to study variability across sites.

software_tool.answer: PCNtoolkit (Predictive Clinical Neuroscience Toolkit); Python 3.6; Nilearn 0.8.1

predictor_variables.answer: Age; Sex; Site of inclusion; FSIQ; ICV

predictor_effects.answer: Age, Sex, FSIQ, ICV, and Site were included as covariates in the Gaussian process regression model. A secondary analysis excluded FSIQ from the covariates.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study appropriately handled multiple nuisance structures: (1) Site/scanner differences were modeled as covariates in the normative model, (2) Age and FSIQ were tested for linear vs. quadratic/cubic effects to handle potential nonlinearity, with linear effects found to be the best fit, (3) ICV was included to account for global brain size differences, (4) Sex was included as a covariate, (5) Quality control procedures excluded subjects with motion artifacts and parcellation errors to handle measurement quality issues.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: A Gaussian process regression model was trained at each voxel in the control cohort using age, sex, site of inclusion, FSIQ and ICV as covariates to predict cerebellar grey matter volume... We tested the best model fit between a linear, cubic, or quadratic model... modeling age and FSIQ with a linear effect was more accurate, as opposed to a cubic or quadratic effect... We performed a careful visual quality check... subjects with >5% missing ROIs excluded... Motion-related artifacts... Euler number threshold... excluded 127 (21%) subjects
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Main paper: Methods line 54-56; Supplement: Methods line 31-32; Results line 194-202

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study used 10-fold cross-validation in neurotypical (control) individuals to assess generalizability and ensure individuals fall within the normative range before retraining on the entire sample. Goodness-of-fit metrics (Rho map showing correlation between predicted and actual values, and SMSE) were computed in the neurotypical subjects.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: To avoid overfitting, assess generalizability, and determine whether neurotypical individuals fall within the normative range, we used 10-fold cross-validation in neurotypical individuals before retraining the model in the entire sample... To evaluate the goodness-of-fit of our normative model in neurotypical subjects, we computed a Rho map of the cerebellum showing the correlation between the predicted and the actual values in the cerebellum. In addition, we calculated the symmetrical mean square error (SMSE) of our model in the neurotypical subjects.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Main paper: Methods line 54-56; Supplement: Normative modeling analysis line 31

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study did not validate the normative model on a completely independent same-domain dataset separate from the EU-AIMS LEAP cohort. Cross-validation was performed within the same cohort.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: No text in the paper describes validation on an independent same-domain dataset of healthy controls separate from the EU-AIMS LEAP cohort.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study performed dimensional analyses in an independent transdiagnostic cohort (Healthy Brain Network, N=352 in relaxed sample, N=79 in stringent sample) with autism-related symptoms, testing associations between SRS-2 T-scores and cerebellar structure. This represents validation on a different domain (transdiagnostic pediatric mental health cohort vs. autism-specific cohort).
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: Dimensional Analyses in a Transdiagnostic Pediatric Cohort: We conducted analyses in the Healthy Brain Network, an independent transdiagnostic mental health pediatric cohort recruited in New York... In this more heterogenous population of individuals with autism-related symptoms without a formal diagnosis of autism, we studied the influence of the clinical dimensions of autism using the SRS-2 T score... We selected individuals with FSIQ > 70 and symptoms related to autism, as defined by SRS-2 T score > 60. We defined both a relaxed (N = 352, SRS-2 T score > 60) and a stringent (n = 79, SRS-2 T score > 76) sample.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Main paper: Methods line 89-92; Results line 113

clinical_dataset.answer: EU-AIMS LEAP (primary); Healthy Brain Network (HBN, validation)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (normative probability maps); absolute value |Z| > 2.6 threshold for deviations

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Linear models including age, sex, ICV, FSIQ, and site as covariates were used to test associations between cerebellar structure and clinical features within autism. Clinical variables tested: SRS-2 T-score (social responsiveness), Short Sensory Profile scale (sensory atypicalities), ADHD DSM-IV rating scale (ADHD symptoms), Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule calibrated severity score, and Restricted Behavior Scale-Revised. Pearson's correlation tests assessed correlations between volumetric measures. Non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney) compared positive and negative deviations between groups. In HBN cohort, linear models tested associations between SRS-2 scores (total, SCI, RRB subscales) and cerebellar anatomy with age, sex, site, ICV, and FSIQ as covariates.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: No significant differences were found in cerebellar anatomy between individuals with autism and control subjects using any analytic approach (linear models, normative modeling, machine learning), and no associations were found between cerebellar structure and clinical features within autism.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Using multiple parcellation methods (CERES and SUIT) and voxel-based morphometry, no significant effects of autism diagnosis were found in cerebellar regions of interest, including the vermis (p=0.38 for total cerebellum with CERES). Effect sizes (Cohen's f²) for diagnosis were all ≤0.002 across all regions. Normative modeling showed no increased or decreased deviations in cerebellar lobules when comparing individuals with autism to controls, despite good model fit (Rho maps showing strong positive correlations, SMSE<1). Support vector machine classification did not predict diagnostic category above chance level (balanced accuracy ≤52%). Heterogeneity-focused analyses found no evidence of cerebellar atypicalities related to sex, age, FSIQ, or clinical features (SRS-2, ADHD diagnosis, sensory alterations, restricted/repetitive behaviors). In matched samples and the independent HBN cohort (N=352 relaxed, N=79 stringent), no associations were found between autism-related symptoms and cerebellar structure. Meta-analysis across six sites showed minimal heterogeneity (I²=0-43%) with only 3 uncorrected findings at individual sites that did not replicate across pipelines.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Several limitations: (1) Concerns about psychometric properties of the Short Sensory Profile scale, (2) 3T MRI may not detect subtle cerebellar differences that 7T MRI might reveal due to partial volume issues in the highly folded cerebellum, (3) The study focused on cerebellar volumetry and did not examine functional or structural connectivity differences that may exist despite normal anatomy, (4) Lower FSIQ and younger age in excluded participants may introduce selection bias, (5) The study included individuals with FSIQ>70, potentially missing effects in individuals with intellectual disability.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: This is the largest and most comprehensive study of cerebellar anatomy in autism to date, using multiple parcellation methods (CERES and SUIT), statistical approaches (case-control, normative modeling, machine learning, meta-analysis), and an independent replication cohort. The authors emphasize that despite a large body of previous literature reporting cerebellar abnormalities in autism from small samples, their well-powered multicenter study found no consistent evidence of such differences. The negative findings were robust across multiple analysis strategies designed to capture heterogeneity, including sex-stratified analyses, age-centered intervals, IQ-centered intervals, matched samples, and dimensional analyses in a transdiagnostic cohort. The authors suggest that previous positive findings may reflect publication bias and false positives from underpowered studies, underscoring the importance of replicability and reproducibility in neuroimaging research.

general_notes.general_notes: This study is notable for its comprehensive methodological approach to address inconsistent findings in the literature regarding cerebellar anatomy in autism. Key methodological strengths include: (1) Large sample size (N=493, with 274 ASD and 219 controls) from six European centers, (2) Use of two independent cerebellar parcellation pipelines (CERES and SUIT) with visual quality control by an expert rater blind to diagnosis, (3) Multiple statistical approaches including traditional case-control, normative modeling with cross-validation, supervised machine learning, and meta-analysis across sites, (4) Comprehensive heterogeneity-focused analyses testing effects of sex, age, IQ, and clinical dimensions, (5) Independent validation in a transdiagnostic cohort (Healthy Brain Network), (6) Rigorous quality control with 21% exclusion rate for motion and parcellation errors. The study's consistently negative findings across all approaches suggest that cerebellar volumetric abnormalities are not a robust feature of autism at the group level. The authors discuss how their meta-analytic approach across sites demonstrates how false positive results can arise in smaller samples with different parcellation methods. Full dataset and site information: Cambridge (45 ASD, 32 controls), King's College London (78 ASD, 55 controls), Mannheim (21 ASD, 18 controls), Nijmegen (77 ASD, 57 controls), Rome (20 ASD, 18 controls), Utrecht (33 ASD, 39 controls). Software tools used include Python 3.6, PCNtoolkit, Nilearn 0.8.1, Scikit-learn 0.24.2, FSL V6.0, Matlab R2017b, Volbrain, and Brainvisa.
